findings.source_passage: said the curate to the barber, 'You will see, gossip, when we are least thinking of it, our gentleman will be off once more for another flight.'
findings.source_locator: paragraph after curate and barber take their leave
findings.why_it_matters: The source includes the curate's closing remark to the barber as direct speech that follows his explicit despair; the draft cuts the framing detail ('said the curate to the barber') and the line about being 'saturated with the nonsense of his unlucky chivalry,' removing the ironic diagnostic voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'saturated with the nonsense of his unlucky chivalry' and the full curate–barber exchange including the curate's prediction that the niece or housekeeper will report what the pair discuss.

findings.source_passage: I promise you, the niece or the housekeeper will tell us by-and-by, for they are not the ones to forget to listen.
findings.source_locator: final exchange between curate and barber before Don Quixote shuts himself in his room
findings.why_it_matters: This dry ironic aside about the women as domestic informants is a minor but distinctive narrative joke; its absence removes a beat of Cervantine irony and the foreshadowing device.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the curate's line about the niece and housekeeper being reliable eavesdroppers to the departing curate–barber dialogue.

findings.source_passage: What do the common people think of me? What do the hidalgos? What do the caballeros? What do they say of my valour; of my achievements; of my courtesy?
findings.source_locator: Don Quixote's long speech demanding Sancho's report, mid-segment
findings.why_it_matters: The source has a formal rhetorical anaphora ('What do… What do… What do…') that is a stylistically distinctive feature of Don Quixote's self-dramatizing voice; the draft collapses it to a plain list ('of my valour, my achievements, my courtesy'), erasing the rhythmic signature.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the anaphoric question sequence ('What do the common people think of me? What do the hidalgos? What do the caballeros?') to preserve the rhetorical register.

findings.source_passage: thou art to tell me, without adding anything to the good or taking away anything from the bad… not allowing flattery to add to it or any idle deference to lessen it
findings.source_locator: Don Quixote's speech to Sancho on truth-telling, before Sancho's report
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is interpretively significant: Don Quixote's explicit demand for unvarnished truth—only to be rattled when he gets it—is a key ironic setup. The draft abbreviates it to a single clause, losing the thematic setup.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Don Quixote's full instruction about not adding to good or subtracting from bad, and the explicit contrast of flattery vs. loyal truth-telling.

findings.source_passage: Is there more, then? … There's the tail to be skinned yet … all so far is cakes and fancy bread
findings.source_locator: exchange between Don Quixote and Sancho before mention of Bartholomew Carrasco's son
findings.why_it_matters: 'All so far is cakes and fancy bread' is a vivid Sanchismo that characterises his idiomatic speech; the draft merges the two lines ('That's just where it is—body of my father!—there's the tail to be skinned yet') and drops the 'cakes and fancy bread' idiom entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'all so far is cakes and fancy bread' as Sancho's colourful vernacular lead-in before the revelation about the published history.

summary: The draft has three medium-severity failures—loss of the curate–barber ironic closing exchange, flattening of Don Quixote's anaphoric self-interrogation, and erosion of his truth-telling speech—that collectively strip interpretive and voice-establishing material warranting regeneration.
